q: Tell me about yourself.
ans: Use a present-past-future structure in 60 to 90 seconds: who you are now (degree, branch, year), the skills and one or two projects most relevant to this role, a strength those projects demonstrate, and what you want to do next. Do not recite your resume or open with family history. Illustrative example (replace every detail with your own facts): 'I am a final-year [branch] student at [college]. I have worked mainly with [skills] and built [project] that [verifiable outcome]. I enjoy [genuine strength], and I am looking to start as a [role] where I can [goal].'
kp: Two or three skills relevant to the role
One project or experience that proves them
Career direction linked to this role
cm: Reading the resume line by line
Starting with childhood or family history
Ending without connecting to the role
fu: Which project you mentioned are you proudest of?
What is one thing that is not on your resume?

q: Walk me through your resume.
ans: Pick a logical thread rather than reading top to bottom: education, then the skills and projects that matter for this role, then internships or activities, then where you are heading. Spend most time on the two items you can discuss in depth and mention the rest briefly. Be ready for the interviewer to interrupt on any line, so include nothing you cannot explain. Illustrative example (use your own content): 'My degree is in [branch]. The most relevant work is [project], where I handled [your part]. Beyond that I did [activity], and next I want to [goal].'
kp: Depth on the two strongest items
Links each item to the target role
cm: Spending equal time on every item
fu: Which line on your resume are you least confident about?
What was your exact contribution to that project?

q: Why should we hire you?
ans: Match three things you genuinely have to three things the role needs: relevant skills, evidence you can learn and deliver, and fit with the team or domain. Read the job description first and use its language. Stay confident without claiming to be the best or putting other candidates down. Illustrative example (replace with your facts): 'The role needs [requirement]. I have worked on [evidence], I learn new tools quickly, as shown by [example], and I would contribute from my first project while growing with the team.'
kp: Mapped to the actual job description
cm: Generic claims such as 'I am hardworking'
fu: Which requirement in the job description are you weakest on?
Can you give evidence for the strongest claim you just made?

q: Why do you want to join our company?
ans: Give two or three specific, verifiable reasons from your own research: what the company builds, its technology or domain, its learning culture, or a published project or engineering blog. Then connect those reasons to your skills and goals. Do not lead with salary or brand name alone, and only state facts you have actually checked on the company's website or official channels. Illustrative example (verify every company fact yourself): 'I read that [company] works on [verified area]. That matches my work in [skill], and I want to learn [specific thing] in a team that does it at scale.'
kp: At least two specific, researched reasons
Linked to your skills and goals
Reasons go beyond salary and brand
cm: Saying the same thing about every company
fu: What do you know about our main products?
What would you want to learn here that you could not learn elsewhere?

q: If two candidates had identical marks and skills, what would tip the decision in your favour?
ans: Avoid claiming superiority. Name one or two verifiable differences: a project that went beyond coursework, consistent self-driven learning, a track record of finishing what you start, or strong communication shown in practice. Support each with a concrete fact the interviewer could check. Close by showing you respect the other candidate. Illustrative example (replace with your own facts): 'Possibly my follow-through. I built [project] on my own, shipped it with [verifiable detail], and kept improving it after the course ended. I can show it if useful.'
fu: How would your teammates confirm that?
What is one area where the other candidate might be stronger?

q: What are your strengths?
ans: Choose two or three strengths relevant to the role and prove each with a short example. Prefer specific strengths such as debugging methodically, learning tools quickly, or explaining ideas clearly over vague ones like 'hard work'. Make sure the example matches the claim. Illustrative example (replace with your own): 'One strength is structured problem solving. When [situation from your life], I [what you did], which led to [result]. I also learn quickly, for example [real example].'
kp: Honest and consistent with your resume
cm: Listing five adjectives with no proof
Choosing strengths unrelated to the job
Naming a weakness disguised as a strength
fu: Tell me about a time that strength failed you.
Which strength would your classmates name first?

q: What are your weaknesses?
ans: Name a genuine development area that is not critical to the job, explain what you have done about it, and show measurable or observable progress. Avoid fake weaknesses such as 'I work too hard' and avoid weaknesses that disqualify you. Illustrative example (choose your own true one): 'I used to hesitate to ask questions, so I lost time on problems. I now set a rule to ask after 30 minutes of being stuck and prepare a clear question, which has made me faster.'
cm: Naming a core job skill you lack
fu: How do you know you are improving?
Has this weakness ever affected a team?

q: What is your greatest achievement?
ans: Pick one achievement you can describe honestly and in detail. Use a short Situation, Action, Result outline, stress your own role, and include a measurable or verifiable outcome. It can be academic, a project, a competition, or a personal effort; what matters is effort, ownership, and what you learned. Illustrative example (use your own real event): 'In [situation] I [your action], and the result was [verifiable outcome]. It taught me [lesson], which I applied later when [real follow-up].'
cm: Describing a team result as solely yours
fu: What exactly was your role?
How did you measure the result?

q: What is your biggest failure?
ans: Choose a real failure with moderate stakes, own your part without blaming others, and spend most of the answer on what you changed afterwards. Interviewers test honesty, accountability, and learning ability, not perfection. Illustrative example (use your own): 'In [situation] I [mistake], which led to [consequence]. I realised [root cause], so I now [specific habit]. In [later situation] that habit helped me [outcome].'
fu: What would you do differently today?
Did anyone else suffer because of it?

q: Tell me about a challenge you overcame.
ans: Select a challenge that required effort and problem solving, such as a technical obstacle, a tight deadline, or a hard subject. Describe the obstacle briefly, the specific steps you took, the outcome, and what you learned. Show persistence and resourcefulness rather than luck. Illustrative example (replace with yours): 'While building [project], [problem] blocked us. I [steps: researched, tested, asked for help], which fixed it and [outcome]. I learned [lesson].'
fu: What alternatives did you consider?
Who helped you and how?

q: Why do you want this role?
ans: Connect the actual responsibilities in the job description to your skills, interests, and learning goals. Explain what draws you to the work itself, not only the title. Show that you understand what the role involves day to day. Illustrative example (adapt to the real role): 'This role involves [responsibility from the JD]. I have enjoyed that kind of work in [real experience], and I want to build deeper skills in [area] by doing it professionally.'
fu: What part of this role do you expect to be hardest?
How does it fit your five-year plan?

q: Why should we invest in a fresher like you?
ans: Acknowledge that freshers need training, then show why the investment pays off: fast learning, up-to-date fundamentals, adaptability, and commitment. Give evidence that you learn independently and have started applying skills. Avoid being defensive about lack of experience. Illustrative example (use your own evidence): 'I understand I will need onboarding. I have shown I can learn quickly by [real example], I have current skills in [area], and I will treat every task as a chance to become independent sooner.'
fu: How long before you could work independently?
What have you taught yourself recently?

q: What motivates you?
ans: Name one or two real motivators that fit professional work, such as solving hard problems, seeing users benefit, steady skill growth, or contributing to a team. Support them with a short real example of when you acted on them. Avoid answering with money or recognition alone. Illustrative example (replace with your truth): 'I am motivated by building things people use. When [real example], I stayed up to finish it because I wanted to see it working for real users.'
kp: Real example of acting on them
cm: Motivators that conflict with the job
fu: What demotivates you at work?
How do you stay motivated on boring tasks?

q: What are your short-term career goals?
ans: Describe the next one to two years in practical terms: becoming productive in the role, strengthening specific skills, and contributing to real deliverables. Make them realistic and tied to the company's work. Illustrative example (adjust to your path): 'In the first year I want to become a reliable contributor on [type of work], deepen my skills in [area], and take ownership of small modules. I would also like to earn [relevant certification or skill] along the way.'
fu: How will you measure progress?
What support would you need from us?

q: What are your long-term career goals?
ans: Show direction without rigid certainty: deepen expertise, grow in responsibility, and eventually mentor others or lead technical work. Keep it compatible with staying and growing at this company. Avoid naming a specific competitor or an unrelated field. Illustrative example (replace with your goals): 'Long term I want to become a strong specialist in [area] and later guide a small team. I will keep learning and take on bigger problems as my skills grow.'
cm: Planning to switch fields or leave
fu: What would you do if the company's direction changed?
Which skills must you build to get there?

q: Where do you see yourself in five years?
ans: Give a grounded picture: a skilled, trusted contributor who owns meaningful work and has expanded into broader responsibility. Link it to the path this company offers and to learning you will actually do. Do not claim a specific title or say you want the interviewer's job. Illustrative example (adapt): 'In five years I see myself as an experienced [role] who owns features end to end, mentors newer joiners, and has deep knowledge of [area]. I hope to build that here.'
fu: What will you do to get there?
What if the growth path is slower than expected?

q: Why did you choose your engineering branch?
ans: Tell the real reason in two or three sentences: what attracted you, how your interest grew, and how it led to your current direction. Show that the choice was thoughtful even if it began with limited information. If it was not your first choice, say so honestly and describe what you discovered. Illustrative example (use your own story): 'I chose [branch] because [honest reason]. In [year] I tried [project/course], which confirmed my interest in [area], and that is why I am applying for [role].'
cm: Saying 'my parents decided' with nothing more
fu: Would you choose it again?
What was the most useful subject and why?

q: What did you learn in college beyond academics?
ans: Choose two or three real lessons such as teamwork on projects, time management, public speaking, or independent learning, and give a brief example of each. Show how these skills transfer to a workplace. Illustrative example (replace with real ones): 'Group projects taught me to divide work and communicate early. Preparing for [event] taught me time management. I also learned to learn independently by [real example].'
cm: Claiming leadership you did not have
fu: Which experience changed you the most?
How did you balance academics with other activities?

q: Can you tell us a little about your family background?
ans: Keep it brief, factual, and positive: who is in your family, what they do in general terms, and how they support your goals. You are not required to share anything uncomfortable or sensitive. Then steer back to your own journey. Illustrative example (replace with your facts): 'My family is from [place]. My parents are [occupation, if you want to say], and I have [siblings]. They have encouraged me to pursue engineering, and I am excited to start my career.'
fu: How has your family influenced your career choice?
Would your family support relocation for this job?

q: Are you willing to relocate for this job?
ans: Answer honestly and clearly. If you are flexible, say so and mention that you have thought about practicalities. If you have constraints, state them calmly and ask about the options instead of giving a flat refusal. Never agree to something you will later refuse. Illustrative example (choose what is true for you): 'Yes, I am open to relocating to [locations]. I would like to understand the timeline and any support for the move.' Or: 'I prefer [city] because [reason], but I am open to discussing other options.'
fu: Which locations would you not consider and why?
What would make relocating difficult?

q: Are you comfortable working in shifts?
ans: Be honest. If you are comfortable, say so and mention anything that supports it, such as having managed irregular schedules during exams or projects. If you have concerns, explain them professionally and ask how the shift roster works. Do not promise what you cannot sustain. Illustrative example (answer truthfully): 'Yes, I can work in shifts if the role needs it. I have managed late-night project deadlines before, and I would like to understand how rotations are planned.'
fu: How would you manage your health on night shifts?
What if the shift changes at short notice?

q: What are your salary expectations?
ans: Research the typical range for the role, location, and company type using reliable sources such as the company's published ranges, recent offers shared by peers, and reputable salary reports, and treat these as estimates. Prefer a researched range or defer politely to the company's structure for freshers. Emphasise learning and fit, but do not undervalue yourself. Illustrative example (use real research): 'I have researched the market for this role and expect a range of [your researched range]. I am open to discussing it based on the role and the company's structure.'
cm: Demanding too much or too little
fu: What if the offer is below your range?
What matters more to you, salary or learning?

q: What would you do if you received a better offer from another company while our hiring process is still ongoing?
ans: Show integrity and clarity: you would compare offers on role, learning, and growth, not only pay; you would communicate honestly and promptly with both companies; and you would not accept and then back out casually. If you strongly prefer this company, say so and explain why. Illustrative example (answer truthfully): 'I would inform both companies about my timeline, compare the roles on learning and growth, and decide professionally. This company is a strong preference because [real reason], so I would ask about your timeline.'
kp: Decision based on fit and growth
cm: Saying you would take the highest pay
fu: What factors would decide it for you?
How would you decline an offer politely?

q: How do you handle rejection?
ans: Explain that you treat rejection as information. Describe how you review what happened, ask for feedback where possible, adjust your preparation, and try again. A brief real example makes it credible. Illustrative example (use your own): 'When I was not selected in [real situation], I asked for feedback, saw that [gap], and spent [time] improving it. My next attempt went better because [result].'
fu: How many times did you apply before succeeding?
What was the most useful feedback you received?

q: Tell me about a time you received criticism and what you did with it.
ans: Use a real example: what the criticism was, your initial reaction honestly, what you did to understand and act on it, and the improvement afterwards. Show that you separate feedback from ego. Illustrative example (replace with yours): 'A [teacher or teammate] told me [specific criticism]. I was disappointed at first, then asked for examples, changed [habit], and later [observable improvement].'
kp: Real criticism, not a disguised compliment
fu: Did you agree with the criticism?
How do you ask for feedback now?
